::: {.why}
A different question from the deflated Sharpe, and a better one: not whether the result is significant, but how often the selection procedure itself picks a loser.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Describe combinatorially symmetric cross-validation in four steps, and say what it estimates that a train-test split does not.
- Compute the probability of backtest overfitting for a parameter search of your own and interpret the number.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Read the probability of backtest overfitting paper, the method section rather than the examples. The idea is to split the performance matrix into all balanced combinations of in-sample and out-of-sample sub-periods and measure how often the in-sample winner underperforms out of sample.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Implement it on a small case: a moving-average crossover on SPY over a grid of 100 parameter pairs, evaluated in 16 sub-periods, then the combinatorial split. Report the probability of backtest overfitting. If it comes out above one half, the search is worse than picking at random, and that is the standard outcome for this particular strategy family.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2017) — The Probability of Backtest Overfitting](https://escholarship.org/content/qt4w1110bb/qt4w1110bb.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}
